title: Reflux confirmation after normal off-treatment endoscopy
fairness: Off-PPI ambulatory reflux monitoring is the best of the offered investigations: the completed mucosal assessment does not establish GERD, and persistent symptoms despite treatment do not supply that diagnosis. Repeating an adequate examination has no stated new indication.

Two consequential steps remain: distinguish treatment failure from objective proof of reflux, then choose diagnostic testing conditions. The on-treatment alternative represents a credible resident error. This is high-yield preintervention workup.

The named 52-year-old woman's presentation and complete task are coherent. The later medication decision follows a completed outside study; this explanation does not disclose that later result or medication answer.

Offline editorial review only: no external source, current numerical criterion, or clinical approval was independently verified. PASS in this report does not change needs_clinician_review; difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments.
suggestions: Optional clarity improvement in a future version: replace 'No ambulatory reflux study appears in the outside records' with the actual verified prior testing history. Absence from a transferred record is not proof that testing never occurred. Both monitoring choices remain plausible from the wording alone, so this is not a key-only omission cue.

title: Medication decision after negative reflux evaluation
fairness: Discontinuing empiric PPI is the defensible best answer among these plans: the four complete off-treatment days show low acid exposure, typical symptoms were captured without positive association, symptoms did not improve on the resumed regimen, and no independent PPI indication is supplied.
The separate-indication check is decision-critical rather than an arbitrary set of distractor-eliminating negatives. No confident clinical error or nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

Two steps are present: interpret reflux burden together with symptom association, then apply that result to medication use while checking independent indications. This is a high-yield refractory-symptom error.

The chronology coherently follows the first node, and the current update plus presentation identify the resumed medication. The first explanation supplies the reason for off-treatment testing but not this result or its management. The later task is complete when shown separately from the presentation.
suggestions: Retain the symptom capture and independent-indication findings. Feedback could explicitly say that persistent symptoms still warrant appropriate evaluation; this result does not establish a particular alternative diagnosis.

title: Junctional metaplasia and surveillance eligibility
fairness: Symptom care without Barrett surveillance is the best answer from the described landmarks and junctional biopsy. The learner must calculate the short displacement and distinguish junctional intestinal metaplasia from an established esophageal Barrett segment.

The outside pathology label is a legitimate competing interpretation, not a supplied answer to the follow-up task. No key-only lexical match or convergence selects the answer without interpreting anatomy.

The ablation option is a weak competitor in a patient without dysplasia or a focal lesion. The surveillance versus no-surveillance distinction remains a credible, consequential high-yield error and supports a moderate judgment, near the easier end.
This is a self-contained single-node case with consistent age, sex and endoscopy history. No prior feedback is required.
suggestions: Preserve measured landmarks and biopsy location. Any future replacement for the weak ablation distractor should be a genuinely plausible follow-up error, with clinical review confirming that it does not create a second defensible key.

title: Recurrent anemia and meal limitation with hiatal hernia
fairness: Offering elective anatomical repair is defensibly best among these plans given the hernia anatomy, contact-site erosions, recurrent deficiency despite treatment, persistent meal limitation, alternative-source assessment and absence of prohibitive operative disease.

The inference is attribution of a clinically important symptom complex to the hernia, followed by treatment selection after medical treatment has not maintained control. Continued medical care is a credible competitor; limited fixation is less compelling for this described operative candidate.

No nonmedical wording attack uniquely identifies the answer. The operative-risk information has a real role in distinguishing definitive repair from limited intervention. This is high-yield paraesophageal-hernia management.

The next node coherently assumes that repair is planned and adds physiological findings. This explanation does not disclose the later fundoplication decision. The current question is complete within the named patient's case.
suggestions: Retain the conditional 'offer' framing and the treatment trajectory; do not turn this into a universal repair mandate for incidentally detected hernias.

title: Reconstruction and reflux control after physiological assessment
fairness: Reduction, hiatal closure and addition of fundoplication is the best-supported offered plan with documented pathological reflux, preserved relaxation and peristalsis, contractile augmentation and no swallowing limitation.

The explanation appropriately describes conditional benefit and dysphagia tradeoffs without asserting that this record mandates a particular wrap or mesh technique. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Two steps are present: interpret reflux and motor findings, then integrate them into the reconstruction. The prior decision to offer repair does not settle the antireflux component. The choices represent distinguishable operations rather than grammatical or label-matching alternatives.

This later node follows the anemia case coherently, provides the current physiological assessment and states its preoperative decision stage. It needs the shared presentation but does not require remembering a previous answer. This is high-yield operative planning.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between supporting a fundoplication and mandating a specific wrap. Preserve the motor findings and swallowing history when composing the case.

title: Selecting reflux-monitoring conditions before a procedure
fairness: Wireless distal pH monitoring off PPI is the defensible best offered strategy when the supplied record contains a normal adequate endoscopy and symptom response but no objective reflux diagnosis. On-treatment strategies answer a different clinical question.

The learner must recognize that partial response to medication and persistent regurgitation do not establish GERD, then select testing conditions that establish untreated reflux burden. This is a narrow but consequential high-yield application.

The key is the sole off-treatment choice, but that distinction is the clinical variable being tested, not a standalone nonmedical clue. Option length and grammar are comparable; the task does not state that testing must be off treatment.

The next node supplies a later completed outside study. This explanation does not disclose its daily values, their interpretation or the motor assessment answer. The patient's presentation and task are self-contained for this stage.
suggestions: A shorter lead-in such as asking which reflux study should precede the procedural decision would read more naturally. Preserve the actual diagnostic-history boundary; do not describe the patient as 'unproven GERD' in visible text.

title: Interpreting daily reflux results before operative assessment
clarityIssues: The task requests a 'preprocedural assessment plan', but one option selects fundoplication rather than an assessment. This unequal decision stage makes it easier to reject without interpreting the record.

cues.why: The task favors an investigation; 'select fundoplication from current studies' is the only option that instead commits to treatment. This partially prefilters the option set.

The key combines the repeated 'Document GERD' classification with the investigative 'obtain' structure used in another option. This incomplete three-option component matrix creates a majority-component shortcut, especially when the treatment-only option is already disfavored by the task.

fairness: The intended clinical answer is defensible: the daily off-treatment pattern establishes reflux under the intended multiday interpretation, while normal endoscopy and barium passage do not establish the motor information required for procedural selection. I identify no confident medical error; the exact numerical criterion was not independently reverified offline.

There are genuinely two potentially consequential inferences, unlike a simple missing-manometry checklist: interpret the variable daily reflux pattern, then recognize the remaining motor-assessment need. The present option construction weakens that intended moderate difficulty.

The chronology is coherent with the earlier off-treatment-monitoring node. Earlier feedback explains test conditions without rehearsing the daily-pattern rule or naming manometry. The shared presentation and later exhibit supply the patient's procedural goal; the task stands alone as a question.
Reflux confirmation and motor assessment before antireflux intervention are high-yield resident concepts.
suggestions: Compare plans at the same decision stage. Use comparably specific assessment plans with clinically credible competing errors; do not leave treatment selection as the only non-investigation answer under an assessment lead-in.

If retaining paired evidence-status and next-action answers, balance their components so majority wording cannot reconstruct the key. Re-solve all resulting options clinically rather than adding a filler fourth choice.
Retain the variable daily pattern and normal-transit findings; those are the useful discriminators. Reapply the cue attack with the numerical exhibit hidden.

title: Additional investigation after inconclusive wireless monitoring
fairness: Off-PPI catheter impedance-pH is the best of these investigations for the unresolved reflux assessment: the multiday record is neither uniformly physiological nor conclusively pathological, and nonpositive symptom association does not resolve that uncertainty.

On-treatment testing assumes a different diagnostic starting point; manometry can serve motor assessment but does not answer the remaining reflux-evidence question. The explanation appropriately says impedance-pH 'can add' evidence rather than guarantee a diagnosis.

Two steps are present: interpret an intermediate, variable multiday result, then choose an adjunct investigation under appropriate treatment conditions. This is clinically relevant, high-yield preintervention evidence assessment; exact adjunct thresholds are not tested here.

The options are parallel investigations. Neither the task nor the exhibit names the keyed modality, and no nonmedical overlap or outlier selects it. The single-node case stands alone with a consistent patient and completed diagnostic history.
This offline judgment does not independently verify the current numerical diagnostic criteria or establish that this is the only acceptable real-world pathway beyond the offered options.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between inconclusive and normal testing, and the limited 'can add' explanation. Avoid turning the adjunct investigation into a universal mandate or a promise of conclusive results.

title: Resolving a dysplasia report attached to a different specimen

cues.why: The task names the target location, and the specimen log labels E17 'tubular-esophageal segment' while J04 is the junction. A reader can select the matching identifier without interpreting dysplasia.

This is the only option that both matches the requested esophageal specimen and reviews a specimen not already named in the GI-pathology addendum. 'GI-pathologist review of specimen J04' repeats completed work; the remaining option acquires new tissue instead of adjudicating the named specimen.

fairness: Expert review of E17 is clinically reasonable and the intended best answer among the choices. The J04 addendum cannot adjudicate E17, and no confident medical inaccuracy is identified.

The problem is cognitive demand: after matching identifiers, the only remaining step is the familiar rule to confirm a dysplasia reading. The record does not force a consequential clinical distinction between adequate existing tissue review and new acquisition; easy administrative matching carries the item.
Expert confirmation of Barrett dysplasia is high-yield, but the specimen-label puzzle does not itself establish resident-level two-step reasoning.
This is now a self-contained single-node case. It does not require the separate downgrade case, and its feedback does not announce that case's eventual grade.
suggestions: Remove the key-only specimen-label route. Compare clinically credible strategies directed at the same relevant esophageal material, with supported observations about adequacy or the actual unresolved pathology question that determine whether review or new acquisition is needed.

Keep any necessary specimen mapping, but make a medical interpretation consequential after the map has been read. Do not add an invented adequacy threshold or falsely imply that a different specimen clears the original dysplasia.
If no supported second decision exists within this objective, propose a deliberately easy confirmation item or merge/park it for manager acceptance instead of calling this moderate.

title: Surveillance after expert downgrade of dysplasia
clarityIssues: 'Routine Barrett surveillance' and 'dysplasia-focused surveillance' name broad categories rather than describe the distinct endoscopic actions or follow-up policies being compared.

cues.why: The authoritative expert result directly negates the option 'Continue dysplasia-focused surveillance'. The remaining record explicitly retains intestinal metaplasia in an esophageal segment, leaving the generic routine-surveillance label with little competing inference.

It is the middle policy between dysplasia-focused follow-up and ending surveillance after the exhibit has explicitly removed dysplasia while retaining Barrett-type tissue. The choices mostly restate the supplied diagnostic categories.

fairness: Continuing surveillance for nondysplastic Barrett is a defensible intended answer after expert review of the same specimen. A negative dysplasia grade does not erase the established esophageal metaplasia. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The supplied expert interpretation does almost all the work. Recognizing that metaplasia persists and following the corresponding surveillance label is one familiar management rule, not two consequential resident-level decisions.
The underlying concept is high-yield, but the flat inspection does not introduce a credible competing action in this option set; deleting it leaves the same answer.
This version is a separate self-contained case, so it avoids the earlier-feedback problem of a direct multipart continuation. That composition repair does not independently make the node difficult.
suggestions: Specify the competing endoscopic actions or meaningful follow-up-policy distinction without inventing numerical intervals.

Require a supported additional finding that changes the decision, such as a genuinely consequential examination or sampling-adequacy issue, while recognizing that the packet already has a dedicated adequacy item.
If this would merely duplicate another node, merge/park it or seek explicit acceptance as a focused easy item. Do not restore ambiguity by hiding the expert review or the tissue location.

title: Surveillance adequacy when negative jars miss the esophageal segment
fairness: Repeating structured sampling of the established esophageal segment is the defensible best answer. The complete collection log and matching accession represent cardia and junction, not the persistent tubular-esophageal columnar segment; the negative jars therefore cannot support stopping surveillance or treating this as an adequate segment assessment.

The completeness statement has a necessary evidentiary role: it distinguishes tissue never collected from an incompletely transferred report. The outside conclusion is explicitly attributed and is a claim to assess rather than a narrator-supplied diagnosis.

Two consequential steps are present: determine the territory represented by the specimens, then decide whether the examination can start a routine surveillance interval or needs completion. This applies high-yield Barrett surveillance and sampling principles.

No key-only phrase or nonmedical option outlier establishes which tissue territory requires sampling. The task and named patient's single-node presentation are coherent and independent of the other Barrett cases.
The explanation appropriately limits the current specimen evidence rather than calling the old diagnosis disproven. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the complete collection/accession record and the previously established esophageal diagnosis. The distinction between repeating an inadequate examination and restarting routine surveillance from it is the valuable competing decision.

title: Negative distal fragments from a longer columnar segment
fairness: Repeat endoscopy with multilevel biopsies is the best offered strategy. The negative fragments cover a small distal part of a longer observed segment, so rereviewing or sectioning the same sampled territory cannot substitute for acquisition from unrepresented territory.

The negative histology remains valid for the submitted fragments; the explanation does not call the specimen useless or assert a confirmed Barrett diagnosis. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Two consequential steps are present: identify a spatial sampling limitation rather than a grading dispute, then choose acquisition rather than further interpretation of the same tissue. Expert review and deeper sections are credible neighboring pathology-workflow errors.

The exhibit does not name the keyed procedure or label the sample inadequate. A reader must interpret coverage and the relevance of patchy histology; the differently worded strategies have comparable specificity. This is high-yield diagnostic sampling reasoning.
This version is a single-node case with consistent landmarks and an unresolved diagnosis. It does not depend on the separate frozen inflammation case or its feedback.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between tissue not sampled and a pathologist's uncertainty in adequately sampled tissue. Do not add a predetermined Barrett diagnosis to the presentation or caption.

title: Completing a post-eradication response assessment
clarityIssues: The presentation does not establish whether this is the first examination meant to confirm eradication or a later surveillance examination after previously documented complete eradication.

'Repeat endoscopy with junctional and distal esophageal biopsies' and 'Continue the scheduled post-eradication endoscopy program' are not clearly mutually exclusive. The scheduled examination could perform exactly the proposed repeat sampling.
fairness: The intended sampling concern is clinically reasonable: the complete negative accession contains cardia and junctional tissue but no distal tubular-esophageal tissue. A squamous-appearing surface does not itself establish a complete histological assessment.

I cannot confidently call continuation of the scheduled program medically wrong from these visible fields. Prior response-confirmation status, the purpose of this examination and what continuing the program entails are unspecified. This is an unresolved option-ranking issue, not a claim that the intended biopsy protocol is inaccurate.

The node has a potentially useful two-step inference: determine represented versus unrepresented tissue, then decide whether the claimed response can be accepted. Its moderate difficulty should come from that evidence interpretation, not uncertainty about the timing of a repeat scope.

Post-treatment recurrence surveillance is high-yield; this particular sampling-protocol detail is narrower. The former highest histology supplies risk context but does not itself settle the repeat-versus-scheduled distinction.

This is now a separate case and coherently states prior resection and ablation. It stands alone from the frozen lesion/resection nodes, but still needs the missing response-assessment stage. No inherited earlier feedback reveals its answer.
suggestions: State whether the current examination is intended to establish complete eradication and whether adequate eradication confirmation has previously occurred.

Make the competing plans distinct at the same stage: completing the inadequately sampled response assessment before accepting its conclusion versus accepting that examination as sufficient for the next routine interval. Ensure every option specifies what happens to the missing distal-esophageal sampling.

Have the clinician confirm the repeat-versus-scheduled ranking from the supported protocol. Do not invent an urgent repeat interval, a numerical surveillance schedule or a stopping rule to force a key.

title: Meal-related breathlessness with an apparent incidental hiatal hernia
fairness: Offering elective anatomical repair is defensibly best among the choices. Meal limitation and reproducible postprandial breathlessness, substantial intrathoracic stomach with adjacent lung compression, unrevealing competing cardiopulmonary studies and preserved independence support a symptomatic hernia rather than an incidental heartburn-negative finding.

Continued observation remains a possible informed patient preference, but the task asks what is most appropriate to offer, not what operation must be performed. Limited fixation has no supplied high-risk or emergency justification. This conditional ranking is fair within the stated choices.

Two steps are present: reassess symptom attribution using chronology, anatomy and competing assessment, then choose the appropriate management offer. Symptomatic paraesophageal-hernia indications are high-yield.

The referral's 'asymptomatic' assertion is attributed to an outside source and contested by actual observations. It does not itself name the operation, and choosing anatomical repair over limited fixation still requires clinical interpretation. No decisive nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

The single-node case stands alone and has a consistent named 74-year-old patient. The explanation appropriately says that a symptomatic hernia is plausible and repair can be offered; it does not claim that causation is proven or every such patient must undergo surgery.
suggestions: Optional tightening: remove the referral's 'because he denies heartburn' rationale, which adds a teaching hint without changing the decision. Keep the actual denial of heartburn only if it serves the intended misconception, and retain the symptom pattern, anatomy and competing assessment.
